notes: A starting grep set, not the rule book. The rule book is whatever fetch_owasp_taxonomy.py
pulled from owasp.org at run time; these patterns only find candidate locations fast.
Each rule carries CWE numbers instead of an OWASP category id, because the scanner maps CWE
to category using the live taxonomy - so when OWASP renumbers its categories, this file
Patterns are cheap and noisy by design: they locate code worth reading, and every hit is
left as verdict=unreviewed for the reviewing agent to confirm or reject. Add rules here when
a repository uses a framework or sink these miss.

rules.title: SQL statement assembled from a string instead of parameters (Python)
rules.explain: The query text is concatenated or interpolated, so any untrusted value in it becomes part of the statement the database parses.
rules.remediation: Pass values as bind parameters (cursor.execute(sql, params)) or use the ORM's query builder; never format user data into SQL text.

rules.title: SQL statement assembled from a template literal or concatenation (JS/TS)
rules.explain: A ${...} or + in the query string means the driver receives a statement whose structure depends on the value supplied.
rules.remediation: Use placeholders with a values array (db.query('... WHERE id = $1', [id])) or a query builder that parameterises for you.

rules.title: SQL statement assembled from a string (Java/Kotlin/C#)
rules.explain: Statement objects built from concatenated text cannot distinguish data from SQL syntax.
rules.remediation: Use PreparedStatement / SqlParameter with placeholders, or the repository layer's parameter binding.

rules.title: Shell invoked from Python (os.system or shell=True)
rules.explain: With a shell in the loop, metacharacters in any interpolated value (;, &&, $(), backticks) become commands.
rules.remediation: Call the binary directly with an argument list and shell=False; if a shell is unavoidable, validate against an allowlist and quote with shlex.quote.

rules.title: child_process exec with an assembled command string
rules.explain: exec spawns a shell, so an interpolated value can chain extra commands.
rules.remediation: Use execFile or spawn with an argument array, and validate any value that reaches the argument list.

rules.title: Shell command built from PHP request data
rules.explain: Request data reaches a shell execution function directly.
rules.remediation: Avoid shelling out on request data; if required, use escapeshellarg with a strict allowlist of commands.

rules.title: Shell command execution (Ruby/Go)
rules.explain: These call a shell; whether it is exploitable depends on where the arguments come from, so the surrounding code needs reading.
rules.remediation: Pass a command plus separate argument list (system('cmd', arg) / exec.Command(bin, args...)) rather than one interpolated string.

rules.title: Source evaluated at run time (eval / exec / new Function)
rules.explain: If any part of the evaluated string is influenced by input, the attacker is writing code rather than supplying data.
rules.remediation: Replace with explicit parsing (json.loads, a lookup table, or a small interpreter for the allowed operations).

rules.title: Untrusted markup sink (innerHTML, document.write, insertAdjacentHTML)
rules.explain: Assigning a string to these sinks parses it as HTML, so any script markup inside it runs in the user's session.
rules.remediation: Set textContent for text, or sanitise with a maintained library (DOMPurify) when markup genuinely must be rendered.

rules.title: dangerouslySetInnerHTML used
rules.explain: This opts the value out of React's escaping, which is the one thing protecting the page from injected markup.
rules.remediation: Render the value as a child instead, or sanitise immediately before the assignment and keep the sanitiser call adjacent to it.

rules.title: Template auto-escaping bypassed (|safe, mark_safe, v-html, triple braces)
rules.explain: Each of these marks a value as trusted HTML, so the template engine stops escaping it.
rules.remediation: Remove the bypass, or sanitise server-side first and document why the value is trusted.

rules.title: Template compiled from a run-time string (server-side template injection)
rules.explain: Template syntax in the string is executed by the engine, which usually reaches arbitrary code in the app's context.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed template file and pass user data as context variables.

rules.title: File path built from request data (path traversal)
rules.explain: Traversal sequences in the value let the request escape the intended directory and read or write elsewhere.
rules.remediation: Resolve the path and verify it stays under the intended root, or map the input through an allowlist of identifiers to real paths.

rules.title: Untrusted data deserialized (pickle / yaml.load / marshal)
rules.explain: These formats reconstruct arbitrary objects, so a crafted payload runs code during loading.
rules.remediation: Use json, or yaml.safe_load; if a rich format is required, sign the payload and verify the signature before parsing.

rules.title: Java object deserialization of external data
rules.explain: Gadget chains on the classpath turn readObject into remote code execution.
rules.remediation: Move to a data-only format (JSON) with explicit field mapping, or install a strict ObjectInputFilter allowlist.

rules.title: Unsafe deserializer (BinaryFormatter / unserialize / Marshal.load)
rules.explain: All of these instantiate types named in the payload, which is enough for code execution.
rules.remediation: Switch to a serializer that binds to a known type, and reject payloads that are not signed.

rules.title: Broken hash algorithm (MD5 / SHA-1)
rules.explain: Both are collision-prone and far too fast; for passwords or signatures this is exploitable rather than theoretical.
rules.remediation: Use SHA-256 or better for integrity, and a memory-hard KDF (argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt) for passwords. Non-security uses (cache keys) are fine - note them as such.

rules.title: Obsolete cipher or ECB mode
rules.explain: ECB leaks plaintext structure block by block, and DES/RC4 are breakable with commodity hardware.
rules.remediation: Use an authenticated mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a unique nonce per message.

rules.title: Credential literal committed to source
rules.explain: A secret in version control is readable by everyone with repository access and stays in history after deletion.
rules.remediation: Move the value to a secret manager or environment variable, then rotate it - the committed value must be treated as disclosed.

rules.title: Private key embedded in a tracked file
rules.explain: Whoever can read the repository can impersonate whatever this key authenticates.
rules.remediation: Revoke and reissue the key, load the replacement from a secret store, and purge the blob from history.

rules.title: Recognisable provider token in source
rules.explain: These prefixes belong to live credential formats, so the string is almost certainly a real key rather than a placeholder.
rules.remediation: Revoke the token at the provider immediately, issue a replacement through a secret manager, and scrub the history.

rules.title: Certificate verification switched off
rules.explain: Without verification, TLS still encrypts but no longer proves who is on the other end, so an interceptor is undetectable.
rules.remediation: Re-enable verification and trust the internal CA explicitly where private certificates are in play.

rules.title: Non-cryptographic randomness used for a secret value
rules.explain: These generators are predictable from a few outputs, so tokens built with them can be guessed.
rules.remediation: Use the platform CSPRNG: secrets.token_urlsafe, crypto.randomBytes, SecureRandom, RandomNumberGenerator.

rules.title: JWT accepted without verifying its signature
rules.explain: An unverified token is attacker-authored: claims such as user id and role can be set to anything.
rules.remediation: Verify with a pinned algorithm and the expected key, and validate iss/aud/exp before trusting any claim.

rules.title: Password compared or stored without a password hash
rules.explain: A direct comparison implies the password is stored recoverably, and MD5 gives essentially no work factor against cracking.
rules.remediation: Store argon2id/bcrypt hashes and compare with the library's constant-time verify function.

rules.title: Debug or developer error mode enabled in committed config
rules.explain: Debug handlers expose stack traces, settings and sometimes an interactive console to anyone who triggers an error.
rules.remediation: Drive the flag from the environment and keep it off by default so production cannot inherit a debug build.

rules.title: CORS configured to allow any origin
rules.explain: Any site can then call the API from a visitor's browser; combined with credentialed requests it is a cross-origin read of user data.
rules.remediation: List the origins that legitimately need access, and never pair a wildcard with credentials.

rules.title: Session cookie missing Secure / HttpOnly / SameSite
rules.explain: Without HttpOnly a script can read the session; without Secure it travels in cleartext; SameSite=None widens CSRF exposure.
rules.remediation: Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (or Strict) on session cookies.

rules.title: CSRF protection explicitly disabled
rules.explain: State-changing endpoints without CSRF protection can be driven by any site the victim visits while logged in.
rules.remediation: Keep the framework's CSRF middleware on; for token-authenticated APIs, document why cookies are not used for auth.

rules.title: Sensitive route with no authorization decorator above the handler
rules.explain: Pattern matching cannot see authorization done inside the function body, so this only flags a place to read - but missing access control is the most-reported OWASP failure and is worth checking by hand.
rules.remediation: Enforce authorization in shared middleware or a decorator applied by default, rather than per handler where it is easy to omit.

rules.title: Record fetched by a client-supplied id with no visible ownership check
rules.explain: This is the shape of an insecure direct object reference; whether it is one depends on whether the surrounding code scopes the query to the caller.
rules.remediation: Scope the query to the authenticated principal (where owner_id = current_user) instead of filtering after the fetch.

rules.title: XML parsed with a default (entity-resolving) parser
rules.explain: Parsers that resolve external entities can be made to read local files or make outbound requests on the server's behalf.
rules.remediation: Disable DTD and external entity resolution (defusedxml, factory.setFeature(DISALLOW_DOCTYPE_DECL, true), DtdProcessing.Prohibit).

rules.title: Server-side request to a URL taken from the client (SSRF)
rules.explain: The server becomes a proxy into its own network - cloud metadata endpoints and internal admin services are the usual targets.
rules.remediation: Resolve and allowlist the destination host, reject link-local and private ranges, and disable redirect following.

rules.title: Redirect target taken from the request (open redirect)
rules.explain: Attackers borrow the domain's credibility to land victims on a lookalike page, which makes phishing and OAuth token theft easier.
rules.remediation: Redirect only to relative paths or an allowlist of hosts; reject anything else.

rules.title: Model updated wholesale from the request body
rules.explain: Fields the client was never meant to set - is_admin, role, balance - ride along with the legitimate ones.
rules.remediation: Copy an explicit allowlist of fields, or validate the body against a schema that rejects unknown keys.

rules.title: Secret or personal data written to a log
rules.explain: Logs are copied to aggregators and retained for months, spreading the secret to systems with looser access control.
rules.remediation: Log identifiers rather than values, and add a redaction filter so a future careless call cannot leak either.

rules.title: Exception caught and discarded
rules.explain: A failed security check that raises and is silently swallowed reads exactly like success, and nothing is logged for anyone to notice.
rules.remediation: Handle the specific error, or log it and fail closed; never let control flow continue as though the operation succeeded.

rules.title: Exception detail or stack trace returned to the caller
rules.explain: Traces disclose file paths, library versions and query fragments, which is reconnaissance handed to an attacker for free.
rules.remediation: Return a correlation id and a generic message; keep the detail server-side in the log.

rules.title: Dependency accepts any version (* or latest)
rules.explain: A floating range means the build resolves to whatever the registry serves that day, including a compromised release.
rules.remediation: Pin a version range and commit a lockfile so builds are reproducible and reviewable.

rules.title: Container image pulled without a pinned tag or digest
rules.explain: An unpinned base image changes underneath the build, so what was reviewed is not what ships.
rules.remediation: Reference an immutable digest (image@sha256:...) and update it deliberately.

rules.title: CI action referenced by mutable branch
rules.explain: Whoever can push to that branch can run code in the pipeline, with access to its secrets.
rules.remediation: Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA.

rules.title: Remote script downloaded and executed unverified
rules.explain: Nothing checks what came back, so a compromised or swapped script executes with the build's privileges.
rules.remediation: Fetch a pinned artifact, verify its checksum or signature, then run it as a separate step.

rules.title: Workload granted host-level privilege
rules.explain: A privileged container is a thin wrapper around root on the node, so one application bug becomes cluster compromise.
rules.remediation: Drop capabilities, run as a non-root uid, and set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false with a read-only root filesystem.

rules.title: Infrastructure exposed to every address or principal
rules.explain: An unrestricted CIDR or wildcard principal removes the network boundary that other controls assume exists.
rules.remediation: Scope ingress to the specific ranges and principals that need it, and keep storage private with signed access.

rules.title: Cleartext http:// endpoint in code or configuration
rules.explain: Credentials and tokens sent over cleartext are readable and modifiable in transit; documentation links are harmless, real endpoints are not.
rules.remediation: Use https for anything carrying data or credentials, and enforce HSTS on services you own.

rules.title: Authentication token kept in localStorage or sessionStorage
rules.explain: Any script on the page can read these stores, so one XSS turns into stolen long-lived credentials.
rules.remediation: Keep session tokens in Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies and keep them short-lived.

presence_rules.title: Environment file committed to the repository
presence_rules.explain: Environment files hold the credentials the application runs with, and committing one shares them with every reader of the repository.
presence_rules.remediation: Remove the file, add it to .gitignore, rotate every value it contained, and ship a .env.example with placeholder keys instead.

presence_rules.title: Key or keystore file committed to the repository
presence_rules.explain: Even when the file turns out to hold only a public certificate, key material in version control is worth confirming rather than assuming.
presence_rules.remediation: Confirm whether the file is private key material; if so revoke it, move the replacement into a secret store, and purge the blob from history.

presence_rules.title: Tool credentials file committed to the repository
presence_rules.explain: These files normally carry registry, cloud or cluster tokens for whoever owns the machine they came from.
presence_rules.remediation: Remove the file, rotate the tokens, and supply them through CI secrets at run time.

pair_rules.title: npm manifest present with no lockfile committed
pair_rules.explain: Without a lockfile every install resolves fresh, so nobody can say which dependency versions were reviewed or shipped, and a malicious release is picked up silently.
pair_rules.remediation: Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci (or the equivalent) in CI.

pair_rules.title: Python dependencies declared with no lockfile or hashes
pair_rules.explain: Unlocked Python dependencies resolve differently over time, which makes a compromised or yanked release hard to notice and hard to reconstruct after the fact.
pair_rules.remediation: Generate a lockfile (poetry/pipenv/uv) or pin with --require-hashes so installs are reproducible.
